verificationRule: An entry may enter agent memory only if it resolves to a live URL owned by an officially-maintained publisher (Shopify, W3C, WHATWG, MDN, web.dev, Google Search Central) or to a named-author study with a citable public page. Anything that fails re-verification is quarantined, never silently merged. Facts are citable; third-party prose is not.

tiers.0: Install now. Official Shopify, executable, zero ambiguity.
tiers.1: Reference codebases. Read and distil. Never redistribute.
tiers.2: Official Shopify standards and tooling. The acceptance bar.
tiers.3: Open web standards. Safe to distil and quote under their licences.
tiers.4: Design evidence. Cited studies and platform-independent research behind the taste rubric. Facts only unless the licence says otherwise.
tiers.5: Legal and licensing boundaries. What the system may and may not reuse.

GraphQL and component code-block validation

teaches: The only codebase Shopify approves for Theme Store submissions
Minimal, unopinionated starting structure for original themes
sources.notes: Binding for Theme Store work. Not binding for bespoke client stores, which is Boldteq's actual business. SKELETON IS THE ONLY SHOPIFY CODEBASE APPROVED AS A THEME STORE SUBMISSION BASE. Submissions derived from Dawn or Horizon are ineligible.

sources.title: Shopify/horizon
sources.license: Shopify proprietary licence (2025-present) with an explicit anti-circumvention clause naming "insubstantial changes, reformatting or reorganizing code" and "claiming independent creation".
teaches: Current first-party theme-block architecture and section-group patterns
sources.notes: Verified from LICENSE.md 2026-07-24. Rights 'may only be exercised to develop themes that integrate or interoperate with Shopify software or services'. You 'may not submit, list, market, sell, distribute, or otherwise make available any theme that is based on, derived from, or incorporates any portion of the Software' - with a narrow exception for delivering to a merchant inside a service engagement, not as a resold product. Read for patterns. Do not vendor into anything we productise.

sources.title: Shopify/dawn

Rights "may only be exercised to develop themes that integrate or interoperate with Shopify software or services". "All other uses of the Software are strictly prohibited."
teaches: Legacy reference implementation of Online Store 2.0 sections and blocks
sources.notes: Dawn's own README still recommends it as a starting point. That guidance is stale for Theme Store submissions. Already vendored at .research/dawn but .gitignore excludes .research/, so it is invisible to git.
sources.correction: This entry previously recorded "MIT / quotable: true". That was wrong and is corrected here. Dawn source may be read and learned from; it may not be redistributed, relicensed, or presented as the basis of a Theme Store submission.

How Shopify bundles section, block and snippet assets

teaches: Which JSON-LD types actually earn rich results, and their required fields

sources.title: Real-Time Detection of Fake-Shops through Machine Learning
sources.publisher: AIT Austrian Institute of Technology / IEEE Big Data 2020
sources.license: IEEE copyright, all rights reserved. Not open access.
teaches: Fraudulent shops are separable from legitimate ones on source-code STRUCTURE alone, without reading content.
Template reuse across shops is the discriminating signal.
Up to 97% accuracy; 48% of fake shops flagged at highest confidence with zero false classifications.
sources.notes: IEEE Xplore returns a bot challenge to non-browser clients; the AIT institutional record is the fetchable publisher-owned URL. This is the evidence that lets AT-1 REJECT rather than warn.

sources.title: Learning DOM Trees of Web Pages by Subpath Kernel and Detecting Fake e-Commerce Sites
sources.publisher: MDPI — Machine Learning and Knowledge Extraction 3(1) 95-122
teaches: DOM-tree structure is more abuse-resistant than content features: text and layout are cheap to change, structural organisation is not.
Accuracy 0.998 at 1,000 training instances; 0.996 at 100.
sources.notes: Openly-licensed corroboration of ait-fakeshop-dom. Prefer this one when the claim needs to be quoted rather than merely cited.

sources.title: Experimental Evaluation of Possible Feature Combinations for the Detection of Fraudulent Online Shops
sources.license: CC BY 4.0 (stated verbatim in the article PDF; the HTML dc.rights meta tag erroneously says 3.0 — a known MDPI metadata artefact)
teaches: Random Forest reaches 0.9693 accuracy on 13-15 features, 0.9342 on the 4 most significant.
Most predictive, in order: domain age, money-back/payment options, top-level-domain length, presence of TrustPilot reviews, logo URL presence.
sources.notes: These are the features a fraud classifier keys on. A legitimate store must not look like this by accident — that is the whole point of AT-3.

sources.title: How Do People Evaluate a Web Site's Credibility?
sources.publisher: Consumer WebWatch / Consumer Reports; research by Stanford Persuasive Technology Lab
sources.authors: Fogg, Soohoo, Danielson, Marable, Stanford, Tauber
sources.license: All rights reserved (© Consumer Reports, Inc.)
teaches: 2,684 people evaluated two live sites each.
"Design look" was the most-mentioned credibility feature, present in 46.1% of comments — rank 1 of 18.
sources.staleness: MAGNITUDES ARE STALE. Run in 2002 on the 2002 web: pre-broadband, pre-mobile, pre-social, US convenience sample. Cite as historical evidence that visual design dominates first-pass credibility judgement. NEVER quote 46.1% as a current effect size.
sources.notes: The Stanford project site credibility.stanford.edu is still live but its own link to the full report is dead; the report now lives on the Consumer Reports advocacy domain. Peer-reviewed companion: Fogg et al., DUX 2003, doi:10.1145/997078.997097.

sources.title: What Makes Web Sites Credible? A Report on a Large Quantitative Study
sources.publisher: ACM CHI 2001; Stanford Persuasive Technology Lab
sources.authors: Fogg, Marshall, Laraki, Osipovich, Varma, Fang, Paul, Rangnekar, Shon, Swani, Treinen
teaches: 1,410 participants analysed (from 1,441 responses). Response scale is -3 to +3.

Item means: physical address +1.86; contact phone +1.71; looks professionally designed +1.55; contact e-mail +1.53; typographical error -1.28; domain name does not match company name -1.06; link that doesn't work -1.45.
sources.correction: An earlier draft of rules/05-ai-tells.md recorded n=1,481 on a -2.0 to +2.0 scale with the item means +1.67/+1.56/+1.54/+1.47/-1.26/-1.07/-1.42. All of that was wrong. The numbers above are read from the authors' own PDF on credibility.stanford.edu and supersede it.
sources.staleness: Same 2002-era staleness warning applies. The ITEMS survive because they are structural; the MAGNITUDES are 25 years old.
sources.provenanceNote: Verified against a single copy (the authors' lab PDF). An independent mirror at inf.utfsm.cl is robots-disallowed and could not be used as a second read. Flagged rather than hidden.

sources.title: Predicting Users' First Impressions of Website Aesthetics With a Quantification of Perceived Visual Complexity and Colorfulness
sources.authors: Reinecke, Yeh, Miratrix, Mardiko, Zhao, Liu, Gajos
teaches: 450 websites, 548 participants, 500 ms exposure.
Colourfulness model r=.88, R²=.78 (adj .77). Visual complexity model r=.80, R²=.65 (adj .64).
Combined with demographics the two models explain 48% of variance in visual appeal (adj R²=.48).
sources.evidenceLimit: ~50% of variance is unexplained. Fitted on 2013-era websites. The score is a signal, never a verdict.
sources.notes: ACM DL blocks automated fetchers; the Harvard author copy is the fetchable canonical mirror. Chosen over a better-scoring CNN because the features are INTERPRETABLE — we can tell a merchant why a page scored low.

sources.title: Webthetics: Quantifying webpage aesthetics with deep learning
sources.publisher: Elsevier — International Journal of Human-Computer Studies 124, 56-66
teaches: A transfer-learned CNN predicts human aesthetics ratings at r=0.85, versus r=0.59 for hand-crafted colourfulness+complexity+contrast features.
usedBy: 04-design-taste §F — the reason we know we are trading accuracy for interpretability
sources.correction: Author list corrected: Dou, Zheng, Sun, Heng. There is no author named Ma.

sources.title: Delving into LLM-assisted writing in biomedical publications through excess vocabulary
sources.license: Paper: CC BY 4.0. Repo github.com/berenslab/llm-excess-vocab: MIT. arXiv preprint 2406.07016: CC BY-SA 4.0.
teaches: Over 15 million PubMed abstracts 2010-2024. At least 13.5% of 2024 abstracts were LLM-processed, up to 40% in some subcorpora.
The style-word frequency jump is abrupt and measurable — larger than COVID's effect on scientific vocabulary.
sources.dataFile: results/excess_words.csv — 900 annotated excess words, 2013-2024, ~39.9 KB. This is the word list AT-9 uses.
sources.ingestRule: Take the MIT-licensed repo CSV, not the CC BY-SA arXiv text. ShareAlike is viral; MIT is not.

sources.title: People who frequently use ChatGPT for writing tasks are accurate and robust detectors of AI-generated text
sources.license: CC0 1.0 Universal — the abs page shows "CC Zero"
teaches: Majority vote of five frequent-LLM-user annotators misclassified only 1 of 300 articles, beating commercial and open-source detectors even under paraphrasing and humanisation.
Experts use lexical AI-vocabulary cues PLUS higher-order signals: formality, originality, clarity.
usedBy: §Z2 why we must not use third-party AI detectors
sources.notes: Public-domain dedication — the cue taxonomy may be copied into memory verbatim.

sources.title: Generative AI enhances individual creativity but reduces the collective diversity of novel content
teaches: AI ideas raised individual novelty 5.4-8.1% but raised cosine similarity BETWEEN outputs by 8.9-10.7% of the human-only similarity range.
The homogenisation is measurable, directional and an explicit social dilemma: each store gets better, the set of stores gets more alike.
sources.notes: This is the evidence that per-store quality checks are insufficient. Quality must be measured ACROSS the portfolio, not only within one build.

sources.title: 10% of E-Commerce Sites Have Product Descriptions That Are Insufficient for Users' Needs
sources.license: All rights reserved. Terms §3.4 forbids copying, reproducing AND PARAPHRASING. Limited citation by permission only.
teaches: 10% of the largest ecommerce sites fail to maintain a consistently high level of product-description detail, driving abandonment.
sources.ingestRule: Store the FACT with attribution and link. Never store Baymard prose, and never paraphrase it into a rule sentence — §3.4 covers paraphrase.

sources.title: Product Page UX 2026: 10 Pitfalls and Best Practices
teaches: 52% desktop / 62% mobile / 64% app ecommerce sites have mediocre-or-worse product-page UX. No site scores perfect.
57% do not use buttons for size selection; 89% do not respond to negative reviews.
sources.deadUrlWarning: DO NOT store https://baymard.com/blog/product-page-usability-report-and-benchmark — the old "82% of sites have severe UX issues" article. It now 308-redirects to a topic listing page. A naive fetch returns the listing's link text and can be mistaken for the article.

sources.title: Visually Reinforce Your Credit Card Fields (89% Get it Wrong)
teaches: Users perceive only PARTS of a checkout page as secure. Card fields must be visually set apart to read as protected.
As of April 2012, 89% of the top 100 grossing ecommerce sites did not visually reinforce the card fields.
sources.staleness: The 89% is a 2012 measurement. The mechanism survives; the percentage does not.

sources.title: "About Us" Information on Websites
sources.license: All rights reserved. NN/g permits quoting "a few words or lines" with attribution and a link; anything more is licensed for a fee.
sources.quotableLimit: A few words or lines only, with attribution and a link back.
teaches: 70+ users observed, 100 sites tested, 65 reviewed, yielding 85 guidelines.
Users cross-check About Us claims against third-party reviews; peer reviews emerged as one of the most important criteria for forming an impression of an organisation.

sources.title: Photos as Web Content
sources.license: All rights reserved. Few-words quoting with attribution permitted.
sources.quotableLimit: A few words or lines only, with attribution and a link back.
teaches: Eyetracking: decorative feel-good images and generic stock people are COMPLETELY IGNORED; information-carrying images of real products and real people are studied closely.
On an Amazon product page 18% of viewing time went to photos, 82% to text.
In a bio layout users spent 10% more time on portraits than on biographies, though the bios occupied 316% more space.
sources.notes: This is why AT-6 rejects stock imagery on EVIDENCE, not taste. The harm is that the image is ignored, so the slot is wasted.

sources.title: Good from Afar, But Far from Good: AI Prototyping in Real Design Contexts
sources.license: All rights reserved. Few-words quoting with attribution permitted.
sources.quotableLimit: A few words or lines only, with attribution and a link back.
teaches: AI prototyping tools follow a general goal but lack the sophistication to weigh design tradeoffs without extensive human guidance.
Output looks polished at a glance while missing visual hierarchy, colour contrast and consistent spacing.
sources.evidenceLimit: No participant count is stated on the free page; methodology lives in a separate companion article. Rated P, not E, for that reason.

sources.title: Prompt to Design Interfaces: Why Vague Prompts Fail and How to Fix Them
sources.license: All rights reserved. Few-words quoting with attribution permitted.
sources.quotableLimit: A few words or lines only, with attribution and a link back.
teaches: Output quality tracks prompt precision. Vague prompts produce inconsistent, unpredictable results and a "Frankenstein layout" that reads as randomly pieced together.
The fix is precise visual keywords, references, analysis, mock data and code snippets.
usedBy: 04-design-taste §A — this is the mechanism behind the four failure modes
sources.notes: Distinct from nng-ai-prototyping; this article cites that one as the prior study. Both URLs independently confirmed live. This is the single strongest argument for a written brief before a build.

sources.title: How to spot a fake website
sources.publisher: Stop! Think Fraud — UK Home Office campaign, GOV.UK
teaches: Public-facing fraud signals: bargain prices with urgency language; bank transfer instead of card; lookalike domains; missing padlock; thin About/Contact; missing returns, privacy or terms pages; poor imagery, layout, spelling and grammar.
Explicit caution that AI now lets criminals produce professional-looking content — so polish alone is not evidence of legitimacy.
sources.notes: The last line matters in both directions: a beautiful AI-built store no longer reads as automatically legitimate to an informed shopper. That is the commercial reason AT-3 and AT-5 exist.

sources.title: How to spot a fake, fraudulent or scam website
teaches: Nine consumer-side signals: lookalike domain and domain age; too-good pricing; bank-transfer-only payment; poor grammar, pixelated images, outdated branding; verifiable phone, email and physical address; shipping/returns/privacy fine print; reviews cross-checked across sources; trust marks verified with the issuing organisation; padlock present but not sufficient.
sources.notes: Current (2026) and consumer-facing, which makes it the freshest available statement of what a shopper actually checks.

sources.title: Colors — Core concepts
teaches: Tailwind v4 publishes its palette in OKLCH, not hex. Stating a hue band without naming the colour space is how this check goes wrong.
The 236-274 degree HSL accent band survives the v3-to-v4 palette change, which is why the BAND is the durable signal and the hex is not.
sources.correction: An earlier draft's exact-hex variant held only v3 hexes (#6366f1, #8b5cf6, #a855f7). A detector holding only those silently stops firing on any v4 store. Both generations are now recorded.

sources.title: Theming — shadcn/ui
sources.license: No licence on the docs page. The shadcn/ui codebase is MIT on GitHub.
teaches: Default (Neutral) base: --primary: oklch(0.205 0 0) in :root and oklch(0.922 0 0) in .dark. Chroma is EXACTLY ZERO in both.
usedBy: AT-12 default framework accent hue — honesty requirement
sources.honestyRequirement: The folk claim that AI purple comes from "Tailwind + shadcn" is half false. shadcn's default primary is achromatic. Never repeat the shadcn half of that explanation.

sources.title: Accessible emoji
teaches: The accessible pattern is role="img" plus aria-label on the wrapping element: ☃.
A bare emoji character has no accessible name and is announced by its Unicode description or not at all.
usedBy: AT-13 emoji standing in for an icon set
sources.notes: This is why AT-13 rejects on ACCESSIBILITY, which is enforceable, rather than on the AI-tell, which is house taste.

sources.title: Refactoring UI
sources.license: Paid commercial product ($99-$149 individual; $399-$2,749 team). All rights reserved.
teaches: Listed so the provenance gate can REJECT it by name. The book's text must never be copied, quoted, paraphrased or distilled into agent memory.
Only one free preview page is publicly readable and even that is copyrighted.
usedBy: AT-14 flat single-elevation, AT-15 hierarchy inversion — as INDEPENDENT house-taste rules, not as derivations of this book
sources.ingestRule: DO NOT INGEST. Where a Polyglot rule happens to agree with this book, the rule must stand on its own stated reasoning and must not cite the book as authority.

rejected.reason: Unmaintained, no dated provenance, majority of links rot. Fails the verification rule.

rejected.pattern: Paid research reports (Baymard Premium, NN/g member reports)
rejected.reason: Licence does not permit ingestion. Free summary pages may be cited for a specific number, never for prose.
Could not be verified on any live Baymard page. The verified figure is 39%. SEO and agency blogs repeat the wrong number. Any rule citing 48% is quarantined.

rejected.pattern: Liquid snippets from Stack Overflow, Medium or agency blogs
rejected.reason: No dated shopify.dev backing. Most predate theme blocks and the 2026 parsing changes.

rejected.pattern: Any theme derived from Dawn or Horizon presented as Theme-Store-ready
rejected.reason: Contradicts the binding Theme Store requirement. See theme-store-requirements.

rejected.pattern: Any claim that Shopify's Dawn theme is MIT-licensed
rejected.reason: Verified false. Dawn's LICENSE.md contains no "MIT License" string and restricts use to developing themes that interoperate with Shopify. This pack previously recorded it as MIT; that entry is corrected, and the false claim is listed here so it cannot re-enter.

rejected.pattern: APCA / SAPC contrast algorithm in shipped code
rejected.reason: Commercial use is prohibited without a signed agreement, and WCAG 3.0 (Working Draft 2026-03-03) does not name it. Use WCAG 2.2 ratios. APCA may be computed for internal comparison only, never shipped and never quoted to a client as the standard.

rejected.pattern: Baymard prose, paraphrased into a rule sentence
rejected.reason: Baymard Terms §3.4 forbids paraphrasing as well as copying. Only the underlying fact may be stored, with attribution and a link.
Dead article URL. 308-redirects to a topic listing; a naive fetch returns the listing's link text and reads like the old "82% of sites" article. Use current-state-ecommerce-product-page-ux instead.

rejected.pattern: Em-dash density as an AI detector
rejected.reason: See rules/05-ai-tells.md §Z1. No validated threshold exists and the false-positive rate on competent human copywriting is unacceptable.

rejected.pattern: Third-party AI-content detectors in the gate stack
rejected.reason: See §Z2. Expert human annotators beat commercial detectors under evasion (russell-ai-detection-cues); the detectors' own error rates make them unusable as a blocking gate.

rejected.pattern: Refactoring UI text, quoted or paraphrased
rejected.reason: Paid commercial book, all rights reserved. Rules that agree with it must stand on their own reasoning.
See §Z3 and 04-design-taste §A. Tuch et al. 2012 and Baughan CHI 2020 show prototypicality dominates complexity in visual-appeal judgement. Penalising "plain" would optimise against the evidence.

licenceClasses.INGESTIBLE: Licence permits copying the text into agent memory with attribution. Prose may be distilled and stored.
licenceClasses.FACTS-ONLY: The finding may be stored as a fact with attribution and a link. The publisher's prose may NOT be copied, stored or paraphrased into memory.
licenceClasses.DO-NOT-USE: Neither prose nor derived text may enter memory. Listed so the gate can reject it by name instead of rediscovering it.

evidenceRatings.E: Evidence-backed by a named study or a binding platform rule. A gate may block on it.
evidenceRatings.P: Practitioner consensus from a credible publisher, without a controlled study behind the specific number. A gate may warn only.
evidenceRatings.H: House taste. Note only. Never described to a client as best practice.
